en: A million-token prompt: about eight terabytes of memory, just to remember it.

That is with the textbook kind of attention, on Llama 3's biggest size, 405 billion parameters: about ten times the model's own weights. So where does that memory go, and how do real models put it on a diet? From Prof. Yufei Ding's CSE 291P, lecture 3.
Quick callback to the last episode. Every token at the attention party carries three things: a question card, its query; a name tag, its key; and a parcel, its value.
To pick the next word, the newest token holds up its question, checks it against every name tag, and takes a share of every parcel.
And a model writes one token at a time. Done the naive way, every time a new token arrives, every earlier token cuts its name tag and wraps its parcel all over again.
But an old token's tag and parcel never change. Same words, same layer, same numbers. Making them again is pure waste.
Her slide says the fix in one line: keep the old keys and values, and only compute attention for the new token.
That is the KV cache. K for keys, V for values. Picture a cloakroom: every guest who came before left a name tag and a parcel on the wall.
The newcomer brings only a question card, reads the wall, and leaves its own tag and parcel for whoever comes next.
Why is there no Q cache? Old questions are never asked again. Only the newest token asks.
The catch: the wall only grows. One more tag and parcel per token, and for every new token, the whole wall is hauled out of memory and read again.
Noam Shazeer wrote in 2019 that this hauling, more than the arithmetic, is what makes generating slow.
So how big does the wall get? Her slide gives the size for one token, as a product. It starts with a two.

Then the number of layers. A model is a stack of layers, each running attention again, so every layer, every floor of the building, keeps its own cloakroom. Then the KV heads. Remember heads from last time: attention runs several copies side by side, and in plain attention each head keeps its own rack of tags and parcels. Then the head size: how many numbers sit on each tag. And 2 bytes per number, at 16-bit precision.
Try Llama 3's 8-billion model, as if it used plain multi-head attention: 2, times 32 layers, times 32 heads, times 128, times 2 bytes.
That is 524,288 bytes. About half a megabyte, for every single token. A 4,096-token prompt: about 2 gigabytes.
Now the 405-billion model: 126 layers and 128 heads. About 8.3 megabytes per token. A million tokens: about 8.3 terabytes.
One note on the slide: its last column mixes units counted in 1,024s with units counted in 1,000s. In plain decimal units it reads 524 gigabytes, 2.6 terabytes and 8.3 terabytes.
That 405B model, released as Llama 3.1, stops at 128K tokens: the million is a thought experiment. So is the plain attention: Llama 3 itself does not use it.

So the fix starts from the formula. Layers and head size come with the model's design. The KV heads are the factor to change. In plain multi-head attention, every head gets a private rack: 32 heads, 32 racks.

Shazeer's idea was multi-query attention. Every head keeps its own question, but they all share one rack: one KV head. The cache shrinks 32 times on the 8-billion model, and 128 times on the 405-billion.
Sharing has a price: quality can drop.
In 2023, Joshua Ainslie and colleagues split the difference with grouped-query attention. Heads form groups, and each group shares one rack.
In their paper, quality stayed close to full multi-head attention, with speed close to multi-query.
Llama 3 keeps 8 KV heads in every size. 32 heads over 8 racks: 4 times smaller. 64 over 8: 8 times. 128 over 8: 16 times.
Back to our giant and its million tokens: from 8.3 terabytes down to about 516 gigabytes.
And one thing her slide stresses: grouping is mainly an inference saving. For the arithmetic, and for training, it changes little.
And memory is the hauling that every new token waits for.
So: keep the keys and values, never the questions. Size per token: two, times layers, times KV heads, times head size, times bytes. To shrink it, let heads share.
Next time: instead of sharing the parcels, what if we zip them?
